title: Unit 15: Modern Physics

topics.name: Radioactive decay and mass–energy
covers: Energy in modern physics (energy in radioactive decay and E = mc²)

topics.name: Photons, blackbody radiation, and the photoelectric effect

guide.title: Modern physics: review guide
guide.intro: Modern physics covers what happens at the scale of atoms and nuclei, where energy comes in packets, particles act like waves, and mass and energy can turn into each other.
guide.equationNote: Constants used in this unit: h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, hc = 1240 eV·nm, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c².

sections.title: Radioactive decay and mass–energy
body: Unstable nuclei decay at random, but a large sample follows a predictable half-life: after each half-life, half of the remaining nuclei have decayed, so N = N₀(1/2)^(t/T½).

In every decay, charge and the number of nucleons are conserved. Alpha decay emits a helium nucleus (Z falls by 2 and A by 4). Beta-minus decay turns a neutron into a proton and emits an electron and an antineutrino (Z rises by 1; A is unchanged). Gamma decay emits a photon (Z and A are unchanged).
points: E = mc²: mass and energy are equivalent. The products of a decay have slightly less total mass than the original nucleus; the missing mass becomes kinetic energy.
A nucleus has less mass than its separate protons and neutrons. This mass defect times c² is the binding energy.
1 u of mass is equivalent to 931.5 MeV of energy.

sections.title: Photons, blackbody radiation, and the photoelectric effect
body: Light is emitted and absorbed in packets called photons, each with energy E = hf = hc/λ. Higher frequency, or shorter wavelength, means more energy per photon.

In the photoelectric effect, a photon gives all its energy to one electron. If hf is less than the metal's work function φ, no electrons leave, however bright the light. Otherwise the fastest electrons have K_max = hf − φ. Brighter light means more photons and so more electrons, but not faster ones.
points: Every object emits thermal (blackbody) radiation. A hotter object emits more at every wavelength, and its peak shifts to shorter wavelengths: λ_max·T ≈ 2.9 × 10⁻³ m·K (Wien's law).
The threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h.
These results could not be explained by treating light only as a wave.

sections.title: Wave–particle duality
body: Light shows wave behavior (interference and diffraction) and particle behavior (photons in the photoelectric effect). Matter does too: a particle with momentum p has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p.
Electrons sent through a crystal or a double slit form interference patterns, which shows that they behave as waves. Everyday objects have wavelengths far too small to notice.
points: Smaller momentum means a longer wavelength.
At the same speed, a lighter particle has the longer wavelength.
Which behavior you see depends on the experiment.
equations: momentum from kinetic energy (at everyday speeds)

example.prompt: Light of wavelength 400 nm shines on a metal with a work function of 2.0 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons.
example.solution: Photon energy: E = hc/λ = 1240 eV·nm ÷ 400 nm = 3.1 eV. K_max = 3.1 eV − 2.0 eV = 1.1 eV.

misconceptions: Brightness sets how many photons arrive; each photon's energy depends only on its frequency.
“After two half-lives, a sample is gone.”
After two half-lives one quarter remains; the amount keeps halving.
“In beta decay, an electron that was sitting in the nucleus escapes.”
The electron is created when a neutron turns into a proton.
Every particle with momentum has a de Broglie wavelength, λ = h/p.

questions.prompt: A radioactive sample has a mass of 64 mg and a half-life of 3.0 days. How much of the radioactive material remains after 9.0 days?
choiceExplanations: 16 mg is what remains after 2 half-lives (6.0 days).
21 mg divides 64 by 3; each half-life halves the amount rather than removing a fixed third.
Halving never reaches zero: after 3 half-lives, one eighth remains.

questions.prompt: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) undergoes alpha decay. What are the atomic number Z and the mass number A of the new nucleus?
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus with Z = 2 and A = 4. Conserving charge and nucleons: Z = 92 − 2 = 90 and A = 238 − 4 = 234 (thorium-234).
choiceExplanations: Z up by 1 with A unchanged is beta-minus decay, not alpha decay.
An alpha particle carries away 4 nucleons, not 2.
This adds the alpha particle instead of removing it.

questions.prompt: In beta-minus decay, what happens inside the nucleus?
choices: A neutron becomes a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino, so Z rises by 1 and A stays the same
A proton becomes a neutron, so Z falls by 1
An electron that was stored in the nucleus is released, so Z stays the same
Two protons and two neutrons leave together, so Z falls by 2 and A by 4
questions.explanation: In β⁻ decay, a neutron turns into a proton. Charge is conserved by emitting an electron, and an antineutrino is also emitted. The nucleus gains a proton and loses a neutron, so Z rises by 1 and A is unchanged.
choiceExplanations: A proton turning into a neutron is beta-plus decay, which emits a positron.
Nuclei do not contain electrons; the electron is created in the decay.
That is alpha decay.

questions.prompt: In a nuclear reaction, 2.0 × 10⁻²⁸ kg of mass is converted into energy. How much energy is released? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
choiceExplanations: 6.0 × 10⁻²⁰ J is mc; the speed of light must be squared.
2.0 × 10⁻²⁸ is the mass itself; it must be multiplied by c².
9.0 × 10¹⁶ is c² alone; it must be multiplied by the mass.

questions.prompt: The mass of a helium-4 nucleus is 0.0304 u less than the total mass of 2 separate protons and 2 separate neutrons. What is its binding energy? (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²)
questions.explanation: Binding energy = (mass defect)c² = 0.0304 u × 931.5 MeV/u ≈ 28.3 MeV.
choiceExplanations: 0.0304 is the mass defect in u; it must be converted to energy with 931.5 MeV per u.
7.08 MeV is the binding energy per nucleon (28.3 ÷ 4), not the total.
3.06 × 10⁴ divides 931.5 by 0.0304 instead of multiplying.

questions.prompt: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 620 nm? (hc = 1240 eV·nm)
choiceExplanations: 0.50 eV is λ/(hc), the ratio upside down.
1240 eV is hc alone; it must be divided by the wavelength.
7.7 × 10⁵ multiplies hc by λ; photon energy decreases as wavelength increases.

questions.prompt: Photons of energy 3.0 eV strike a metal with a work function of 2.3 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons?
questions.explanation: K_max = hf − φ = 3.0 eV − 2.3 eV = 0.70 eV.
choiceExplanations: 5.3 eV adds the work function; the electron must use that energy to escape.
2.3 eV is the work function, the energy needed just to escape the metal.
The photon energy is above the work function, so electrons are ejected with some kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: Light whose frequency is below a metal's threshold frequency shines on the metal. The light is made much brighter. What happens?
choices: Electrons are ejected once the light is bright enough
Electrons are ejected after the metal absorbs light for long enough
More electrons are ejected, each with less kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Each photon gives its energy to one electron. Below the threshold frequency, no single photon has enough energy for an electron to escape. Brighter light means more photons, but each one still falls short.
choiceExplanations: Brightness changes the number of photons, not the energy of each one.
An electron cannot store up energy from several photons; each photon acts alone.
Below the threshold frequency no electrons are ejected at all.

questions.prompt: A star's thermal radiation peaks at a wavelength of 500 nm. Using Wien's law, λ_max·T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m·K, what is its surface temperature?
choiceExplanations: 5.8 × 10⁶ K results from writing 500 nm as 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; 500 nm is 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m.
1.5 × 10⁻⁹ K multiplies the constant by the wavelength; T is the constant divided by λ_max.
580 K results from writing 500 nm as 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ m.

questions.prompt: An electron has a momentum of 6.63 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
questions.explanation: λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)/(6.63 × 10⁻²⁴) = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, about the size of an atom.
choiceExplanations: 4.4 × 10⁻⁵⁷ multiplies h by p; the wavelength is h divided by p.
1.0 × 10¹⁰ is p/h, the ratio upside down.
6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ is h alone; it must be divided by the momentum.

questions.prompt: Which observation shows that electrons can behave as waves?
choices: Electrons passing through a crystal produce a diffraction pattern
Light ejects electrons from a metal surface (the photoelectric effect)
Some nuclei emit electrons in beta decay
Electrons are deflected by a magnetic field
questions.explanation: Diffraction and interference are wave behaviors. When electrons pass through the regular arrangement of atoms in a crystal, they form a diffraction pattern, just as light does through a grating.
choiceExplanations: The photoelectric effect shows that light behaves as particles (photons), not that electrons behave as waves.
Beta decay shows that electrons can be created in nuclear decay, not that they behave as waves.
Deflection by a magnetic field is particle behavior: a moving charge feeling a force.

questions.prompt: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. The proton's mass is about 1836 times the electron's. Which has the longer de Broglie wavelength, and by about how much?
choices: Neither: equal kinetic energies give equal wavelengths
questions.explanation: λ = h/p and p = √(2mK). With the same K, λ ∝ 1/√m, so the electron's wavelength is √1836 ≈ 43 times longer.
choiceExplanations: 1836 is the ratio for equal speeds; with equal kinetic energies the ratio is the square root of the mass ratio.
The heavier proton has the larger momentum, so its wavelength is shorter, not longer.
The wavelength depends on momentum, and equal kinetic energies give different momenta for different masses.
